title: AI Is Planning Your Guests' Trips. Is Your Resort on the Itinerary?
seoTitle: AI Trip Planning: Is Your Resort on the Shortlist?
seoDescription: Travelers now ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode and Perplexity to plan whole trips. A 10 minute check to see if your resort or hotel makes the shortlist.
excerpt: Travelers ask AI to plan the whole trip, and it picks a few properties. Here is a 10 minute check to see whether your resort makes that shortlist.
imageAlt: Woman in a white shirt sitting at the edge of a resort pool with her feet in the water, typing on a laptop
imageIdea: Real photo of a traveler planning on a laptop at a resort pool, no faces and no visible brand logos.
author: The SocialDM Insights Team
bodyHtml:
More travelers now hand the whole trip to an AI assistant. They type something like "plan a spa weekend in Scottsdale" or "best adults only resort near Phoenix with a great pool," and the answer comes back as a short itinerary with two or three properties already chosen. If your resort or boutique hotel is not one of them, that guest may never see your website. You lose them before the comparison starts.

You can see where you stand in about ten minutes, and most of what these tools appear to lean on is already in your team's hands.

How are travelers using AI to plan trips now?

Quickly, and in growing numbers. Phocuswright's AI Surge report from March 2026 found that 56% of the travelers it surveyed used AI for planning, booking or in destination help on at least one trip in the past 12 months, up from 33% in the first half of 2025.

Google is building trip planning straight into Search. Its post on planning travel with Canvas in AI Mode describes a traveler describing a trip and getting a custom itinerary in a side panel, with flight and hotel options and local attractions laid out on a map. Google has also explained how to book travel with AI Mode: a traveler can compare hotels with guest reviews and, with partners such as Booking.com, Expedia, Hilton, IHG and Marriott, continue to booking without leaving Google. It is rolling out in the U.S. in English.

Not every traveler wants AI to finish the job. Expedia Group's AI Trust Gap research found that 40% of the people it surveyed would use AI to build itineraries, while 66% said they would not trust AI to book on their behalf. On the OpenAI side, Skift reported in March 2026 that OpenAI walked back plans for checkout inside ChatGPT, shifting it back toward discovery.

Booking may still happen on a site the traveler trusts. The shortlist, though, is increasingly written by AI.

Why is the AI shortlist such a big risk for resorts?

Because a shortlist is short. A search results page gave travelers a long scroll and a map full of pins. A trip plan gives them a handful of names with reasons attached.

That changes the competition. You are competing for one of a few seats in a recommendation, against the comp set you already watch for rate and occupancy. If a competitor is named for "romantic resort with a spa near Sedona" and you are not, the guest who wanted exactly what you offer may book them without ever knowing you existed.

It also changes who gets the booking. When AI Mode lets a traveler continue to book through large partners, a property that is named but poorly represented on its own channels can end up booked through an agency. Our post on winning direct bookings from Google covers that side of the problem.

How do you run a 10 minute AI trip planning check?

Open each assistant in a private browser window, signed out where you can, and ask the trip planning questions your guests would actually ask. Leave your property name out of the first round, because the point is to see whether you are chosen when nobody asks for you.

Trip typeExample promptWhat it tests
StaycationPlan a spa weekend in Scottsdale for two adults next monthWhether you make a local drive market shortlist
Amenity ledBest adults only resort near Phoenix with a great poolWhether your signature amenities are known and believed
OccasionPlan a quiet anniversary trip to Sedona with a nice dinner on siteWhether the AI connects you to the reason for the trip
Budget and feesBoutique hotel in Old Town Scottsdale without a resort feeWhether your fees and policies are described accurately

Swap in your own destination. Run each prompt in ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode and Perplexity. For each answer, note three things: which properties are named, in what order, and which sources are cited or linked. Then ask "tell me about [your resort]" to check the facts.

Answers vary between sessions, so treat one check as a snapshot and repeat the same prompts monthly.

How should you read the results against your comp set?

List the four to six properties a guest would really weigh you against. Then count, across all your prompts and all four tools, how often each one was named.

  • You are named about as often as your competitors. You have a fair share of the shortlist. Check that the reasons match what you want to be known for.
  • You are named for some trips but not others. The AI may know you for one thing, such as the spa, and not another, such as the pool or the dining. That is a specific gap.
  • A competitor is named far more often. Look at the sources cited for them. They show which guides and review sites these tools read in your market.
  • You are named with wrong facts. An old resort fee or a closed restaurant can talk a guest out of you. Fix those first.

What signals appear to shape which properties get picked?

No AI company publishes a formula for trip plans, so treat this as what the evidence suggests, not a guarantee.

  1. Review themes. Assistants often explain a pick with what guests say, such as "quiet" or "the pool gets crowded." The themes in your reviews become the reasons you are, or are not, recommended. We wrote more on this in how guest reviews shape where travelers stay.
  2. Accurate amenities. Google's help page on managing your hotel's details says verified hotels can edit amenities in the Business Profile, and that you can correct amenity information Google has summarized if it is wrong. If your spa is not clearly listed, an AI has less reason to match you to a guest asking for one.
  3. Policies and fees. Google's price accuracy policy expects mandatory fees to be disclosed and the total on your booking page to match what Google shows.
  4. Rich property pages. Separate, plain text pages for rooms, the spa, the pool, dining, packages and policies give it facts it can use. Google's AI features documentation says a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode.
  5. Third party travel coverage. Traced citations often lead to travel guides, tourism pages and editorial roundups. If competitors appear there and you do not, that gap tends to show up in AI answers.

What does good look like?

A resort in good shape shows up in the trip plans that match what it actually sells. It is named for its real strengths, and the reasons sound like its best reviews. When a traveler asks a follow up, the answer gets the fees, policies and amenities right. And the path back to its own booking engine is easy to find.

Good does not mean being named for every prompt. It means winning the trips you were built for, at least as often as the competitors guests compare you with.

What should a GM or owner do this week?

Run the check yourself, with your own comp set. Seeing a competitor named for a trip you host every weekend makes the issue real quickly. Then share the results with whoever owns your website, Google Business Profile and reviews.

Questions we hear

Can a resort pay to be included in AI trip plans?

Skift reported that OpenAI began piloting ads in ChatGPT in 2026, but the recommendations themselves depend on what an assistant finds and trusts about you.

Which AI tools should a hotel check?

At minimum ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode and Perplexity. Use the same prompts in each and note who is named and which sources are cited.

Do travelers actually book through AI?

Some do, through options such as partner booking in Google AI Mode. Expedia Group's research found many travelers still prefer to book with brands they trust, which makes the AI shortlist the place where the decision often starts.

Why does AI recommend a competitor with fewer amenities?

Often because its amenities, reviews and policies are easier to find and confirm. Check that yours are clear on your Google Business Profile and website.

How often should we run the trip planning check?

Monthly, and again after a renovation, new amenity, fee change or rebrand. Keep the prompts identical.

takeaways: Travelers increasingly ask AI to plan the whole trip, and the answer names only a few properties.
Phocuswright found 56% of travelers it surveyed used AI on at least one trip in the past 12 months, up from 33% in early 2025.
Run unbranded trip planning prompts in ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode and Perplexity and count how often you and your comp set are named.
Review themes, accurate amenities, clear fees and policies, rich property pages and third party travel coverage appear to shape who gets picked.
Good looks like being named for the trips you were built for, with correct facts, at least as often as your competitors.
